system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2158-10-03 04:56:00 to 2158-10-10 11:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for diabetic ketoacidosis with hyperglycemia, abdominal pain, and purulent drainage from her GJ tube site. She was stabilized in the ICU with an insulin drip and IV fluids, resolving her DKA. During the hospitalization, the external portion of her GJ tube was found disconnected, and a fractured segment was retained in the stomach. She underwent a successful radiologically guided procedure to remove the fragment and replace the GJ tube. She improved clinically, tolerated oral intake, and was discharged home with updated insulin therapy, pain medication supply for her scheduled pain clinic visit, and instructions for tube site care. Her mental health and compliance were supported throughout by her medical guardian.
problems: Diabetes with ketoacidosis, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Mechanical complication of colostomy and enterostomy
Attention to other artificial opening of digestive tract

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ woman who presented with DKA, please perform focused
oblique x-ray to evaluate for any obstruction of port.

COMPARISONS:  Portable AP radiograph from ___.

FINDINGS:  Oblique views demonstrate a right chest port catheter with no
detectable abnormality at the point of connection of the catheter with the
port.  There is possibly a kink between the clavicle and the first rib.  The
tip terminates in the mid SVC.  There is no focal consolidation, pleural
effusion or pneumothorax.  The cardiomediastinal silhouette is unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:  No abnormal connection of catheter with port.  Possible kink in
the mid-portion of the catheter.

PORT CHECK FROM ___

HISTORY:  ___ woman with diabetes/hx DKA and difficulties with venous
blood draws, who had a port placed at outside institution.  Patient is now
complaining of severe pain around the port with flushes and infusions.  Plain
films show question of pinch-off syndrome.

OPERATOR:  Dr. ___.

ANESTHESIA:  None.

TECHNIQUE:  Prior to the study, the procedure and alternatives and risks were
discussed with the patient by ___, PA, and consent was signed.  In
interventional radiology, the patient was placed supine on the table, and a
preprocedure huddle and timeout were performed per ___ protocol.  A scout
image was obtained over the right side of the chest and abdomen.  The port,
which had been previously accessed by ___, RN, was hooked to a
sterile contrast syringe, aspiration was performed and then injections were
performed with storage of fluoroscopy images, still images and two DSA runs,
all with hand injection.  Based on the results of this, the port was flushed
with 6 cc of sterile saline.

FINDINGS:  Scout image shows apparent looping of the proximal tubing of the
port which appears to be related to the overlying soft tissues.  The tip of
the tubing ends at the level of the proximal right atrium.  Injected contrast
exits briskly at the distal end and no leak is seen via the more proximal
portion of the tubing or around the port.  The port reservoir is seen to fill
in its entirety.  There is evidence of a short segment of fibrin sheath with
backflow of contrast along the distal 1 cm of tubing, but this does not extend
up any more proximally or inhibit brisk forward flow of contrast.  Blood was
easily obtained upon aspiration.  Note that the patient described severe pain
with each port injection including moderate pain with the flush at the end.
Contrast is seen in G-tube retention balloon.

CONCLUSION:  Portogram showing no leak or obstruction.  Short segment of
fibrin sheath is not inhibiting forward flow of contrast.  Based on the
results of plain upright chest radiograph showing possible pinch-off and the
patient's symptoms, the patient may return for port removal and replacement.

PROCEDURES:
1.  Placement of a double-lumen chest port via the left internal jugular vein.
2.  Removal of existing right subclavian chest port.

CLINICAL INDICATION:  ___ woman with kinked existing right-sided chest
port and pain with existing port injection.  Flow study performed on ___
demonstrated no extravasation from existing port; however, the patient had
significant pain with injection and flushing.

Informed consent for both procedures was obtained after risks, benefits, and
potential complications had been discussed.  The patient was placed on the
angiographic table in supine position.  The skin of bilateral anterior chest
wall and of the left anterior neck was prepped and draped in a sterile
fashion.  Timeout protocol was carried out prior to the procedure according to
the ___ policy.

ANESTHESIA:  General endotracheal.

LOCAL ANESTHESIA:  20 mL of 1% lidocaine without and with epinephrine.

Under real-time ultrasound guidance, the left internal jugular vein was
punctured using 21-gauge micropuncture needle.  Over a 0.018 guidewire,
micropuncture needle was exchanged for a 4 ___ micropuncture sheath
followed by advancement of 0.035 ___ guidewire into the inferior vena cava.
The right port was then removed as described below.  Attention was then
diverted to the left anterior chest wall.  A linear incision was made,
inferolateral to the left internal jugular venipuncture.  After generous
infiltration of the subcutaneous tissues of the chest wall by 1% lidocaine,
using blunt dissection technique, a soft tissue pocket was created caudad to
the chest wall incision.  A double-lumen chest port was assembled and flushed
and tested for integrity.  The port was implanted into the pocket and secured
to the chest wall using 0 Prolene sutures.  Associated soft tissue tunnel was
created between the chest wall incision and left internal jugular
venipuncture.  A double-lumen permanent catheter was pulled through the
tunnel.  After appropriate dilatation of the needle tract, the permanent
catheter was advanced into the right atrium through the appropriate peel-away
sheath which was subsequently removed.  Chest wall incision was closed in
layers using 2 and 4 Vicryl suture.  Left internal jugular venipuncture was
closed using 4 Vicryl suture.  Both lumens of the port were accessed using
___ needles.  Chest port was covered with sterile dressing.

RIGHT-SIDED CHEST PORT REMOVAL:  This removal was performed after placement of
___ wire from left IJ. After generous infiltration of the subcutaneous soft
tissues overlying the existing right subclavian chest port by 1% lidocaine
with epinephrine, a linear incision was made overlying the chest port.  The
port was dissected from the chest wall and freed of the fibrous capsule. 
Permanent catheter was pulled from the right subclavian vein.  Chest wall
incision was closed in layers and covered with sterile dressing.

Dr. ___, the attending physician, supervised the procedure.

CONCLUSION:

1.  Uncomplicated placement of the double-lumen chest port into the right
atrium via the left internal jugular vein.

2.  Both chambers of the port are accessed and ready to use.

3.  Uncomplicated removal of the right chest port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this awful stomach pain for three days. It’s in my upper belly and goes to my back. I can’t eat, I’ve been throwing up, and I just feel so weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, low-grade fevers—around 100 to 101. And night sweats. I’m also worried my GJ tube site might be infected again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We checked your blood sugar in the ER—it was very high, 764. And your labs show some acid buildup, which suggests diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my urine didn’t show ketones. Does that mean it’s not DKA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Sometimes with poor blood flow or dehydration, ketones don’t show up in urine even if DKA is starting. Your blood work still shows signs of it, so we’re treating it just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you IV fluids and insulin to bring your sugar down safely. We’ll also keep an eye on your electrolytes and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar has come down to 433 after the first insulin dose. That’s improving. We’ll keep adjusting the insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it because I haven’t been eating? I haven’t taken my insulin either—I just didn’t feel like it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Not eating and skipping insulin can throw your sugars way off, even without infection. We’ll work with the diabetes team to adjust your plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My port hurts when they try to flush it. It’s been burning for weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll order an X-ray to check if there’s a kink or blockage. That could explain the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray shows a possible kink in the catheter near your collarbone. We’re going to do a port study to check the flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might feel some pressure, but we’ll go slow. The radiologist will explain everything before starting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The port study didn’t show a leak, but you had severe pain during the flush. The X-ray suggests pinch-off syndrome—where the catheter gets compressed between bones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why it hurts? What can we do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend removing the old port and putting in a new one on the other side. A double-lumen port will give us better access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s done under general anesthesia. The surgery team will take care of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar is still high this morning—403. We’re increasing your insulin dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel shaky sometimes. Is that the insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re watching closely. Your levels are coming down steadily, which is good. We’ll keep adjusting to avoid lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My magnesium was low yesterday. Did you fix that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we gave you supplements. Your latest level is better, but still a bit low. We’ll keep giving it through the IV for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your anion gap has closed, and your bicarbonate is normal. That means the DKA is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m out of the woods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that part is under control. Now we’re focusing on your port surgery and making sure your pain is managed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about the surgery tomorrow. Will I be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure is routine. You’ll be asleep, and the team does this often. The old port is causing pain, so replacing it should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from surgery. The procedure went perfectly. We removed the old port from your right side and placed a new double-lumen one in your left neck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurts a little, but not like before. Is it safe to use already?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both chambers are working. We’ll start using it for meds and labs. You should feel much better with the new one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My calcium dropped today. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s low, but we’re giving you supplements. It’s likely related to your chronic pancreatitis and nutrition. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking good. Blood sugar is stable, electrolytes are improving, and you’re tolerating food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We want to make sure your pain is controlled and you’re comfortable with your insulin again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m supposed to get my pain meds renewed soon. Will you give me a new prescription?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on your regular pain meds here, but we won’t give a new prescription. Your contract is with your PCP, and they’ll handle the renewal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using my albuterol more. I feel a little short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oxygen levels are normal, and lungs are clear. It might be from anxiety or pain. Keep using your inhaler as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to change my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The diabetes team adjusted your sliding scale. We’ll give you a sheet to take home with the new instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I feel better, but I was worried about the port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The new port is working well. Just keep the site clean and let your doctor know if it becomes red or painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I don’t want another DKA episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your glargine at bedtime and use the sliding scale with meals. Eat regularly—even if you’re not hungry—and don’t skip doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your usual hydrocodone and ibuprofen as prescribed. Your PCP will handle the refill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the port? Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid heavy lifting for a few days. Otherwise, you can use it normally. The nurse will go over care before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really scared this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You did well. Just follow up with your doctors and call if your sugar goes too high or low, or if you have pain with the port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I stop smoking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It would help your diabetes and overall health. We can give you resources if you’re ready to try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe I will. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great step. Let your PCP know—they can support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, the discharge papers are ready. The nurse will bring them shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your time getting home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Goodbye.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for abdominal pain and found to have diabetic ketoacidosis with a blood glucose of 764 and mild anion gap metabolic acidosis. She was treated with IV insulin and fluids, which resolved the DKA. During the hospitalization, she reported pain with port access, and imaging revealed a kinked catheter consistent with pinch-off syndrome. She underwent successful removal of the dysfunctional right subclavian port and placement of a new double-lumen port in the left internal jugular vein. Her pain was managed per her care contract, and electrolyte imbalances, including low magnesium and calcium, were corrected. She stabilized clinically, tolerated oral intake, and was discharged home with updated insulin instructions, continued pain medications, and follow-up planned with her primary care provider for medication renewal and smoking cessation support.
